seo.title: Control System Retrofit & PLC Migration — PLC-5, SLC 500, S5
seo.description: Retrofit obsolete machine controls instead of replacing the machine. PLC-5, SLC 500, Siemens S5 and relay-logic migration, new UL 508A panel, HMI with recipes, drives, distributed I/O and on-site cutover — typically one weekend of downtime. System integration for customer-built machines.

schema.name: Machine control retrofit and system integration

sections.title:
The machine is fine.
The controls are *from 1994*.
sections.text: A mechanically sound machine with a dead PLC is not a machine you have to replace. We strip the obsolete controls and electrical system out, design and build a new one around current components, write the code, and start it up on your floor — often for a fraction of what the replacement machine costs, and without retraining anyone on new mechanics.

sections.heading: Old controls, or no controls
sections.intro: Both start the same way — an engineer walks the machine with you — but they're different scopes and they get quoted differently.

cards.title: Control system retrofit
cards.text: The machine still does its job mechanically. The controls are obsolete, unsupported, or failing — and the person who understood the old program has retired.

sections.intro: None of these stop working the day they're discontinued. What happens is quieter: spare parts move to the used market, prices climb, support ends, and a failure that used to mean an afternoon becomes a six-week hunt on eBay. The time to retrofit is while the machine is still running.

sections.eyebrow: The part everyone actually worries about
sections.heading: How long is my line down?
sections.intro: This is the real question behind every retrofit quote, and most integrators answer it vaguely. We plan the cutover before we quote, because the answer determines whether the project is worth doing at all. The new panel is built, wired, and fully tested in our shop against a simulated machine — so the work that happens on your floor is disconnect, mount, land wires, and start up.

sections.heading: When the machine is too long to bring to us
sections.intro: Plenty of the equipment we retrofit can't be crated and shipped — it's 20, 40, 60 feet of line bolted to a plant floor. That changes the electrical architecture, not just the logistics.

cards.title: One central panel
cards.text: Every sensor, valve, and motor home-runs back to a single enclosure at one end of the machine.

lists.heading: What that costs you
items: Hundreds of long wire runs end to end
Large conduit and cable tray fills
Days of on-site pulling and terminating
A fault at one end means walking to the other to troubleshoot
Adding a device later means a new run the full length

cards.title: Distributed I/O over Ethernet
cards.text: Small I/O nodes placed local to the devices they serve, linked back to the controller on a single industrial Ethernet run.

lists.heading: What changes
items: Field wiring drops to short local runs
One network cable replaces the bundle down the machine
Install time and conduit cost fall sharply
Node-level diagnostics — the network tells you which section faulted
Adding a device later means wiring to the nearest node
Sections can be commissioned independently during cutover

sections.note: EtherNet/IP, EtherCAT, PROFINET, or your existing plant standard. Architecture is decided during the survey, before the quote.

items.q: Should I retrofit or just buy a new machine?
items.a: It depends almost entirely on the mechanical condition. If the frame, drives, and tooling are sound and the machine still makes good parts, a retrofit typically runs a fraction of replacement cost, keeps a footprint your plant is already laid out for, and doesn't require retraining operators on new mechanics. If the mechanics are worn out or the process itself needs to change, a retrofit is money spent on a machine that will still be limited afterward — and we'll tell you that during the survey.

items.q: We have no drawings for this machine. Can you still do it?
items.a: Yes, and it's extremely common. Part of the survey is reverse engineering what's actually installed rather than what someone thinks is installed. You end up with a complete AutoCAD package — frequently the first accurate documentation the machine has ever had, which is worth something on its own the next time anything goes wrong.

items.q: How long will my line actually be down?
items.a: For most retrofits, one planned weekend or maintenance window. That's achievable because the panel is built and the code is written and simulated before anyone touches your machine. We commit to a downtime window in the quote rather than discovering it during the shutdown — and if a machine can't be done in a weekend, you'll hear that before you sign, not after.

items.q: Can you write recipes for different products?
items.a: Yes, and it's usually one of the biggest practical wins of a retrofit. Instead of an operator dialing in settings from memory or a laminated sheet, product parameters get stored, named, version-controlled, and recalled from the HMI. Changeover gets faster and far more repeatable, and it removes a common source of scrap.

items.q: Do you do the field wiring, or do we hire an electrician?
items.a: We do it. Our technicians handle on-site wiring, integration, and startup, which matters more than it sounds — when the people who designed the panel are the ones landing the wires, problems get solved on the spot instead of turning into a scheduling conversation between two vendors.

items.q: What if we already built the machine ourselves?
items.a: That's Path B, and it's a large share of our work. Send us the mechanical system and a description of how it should behave, and we handle the electrical design, panel, programming, recipes, and field integration. You don't need a written spec to start — a walkthrough of the machine is usually enough.

sections.heading: Send a photo of the panel. That's genuinely enough to start.
sections.intro: Most retrofit conversations begin with someone photographing the inside of an old control cabinet on their phone. If you can add any of the below, the assessment gets sharper.

checklist.title: Photos of the existing panel and machine
checklist.hint: Door open, plus a wide shot of the machine

checklist.title: PLC and drive part numbers
checklist.hint: Read them off the labels — that alone tells us a lot

checklist.title: Any drawings you have
checklist.hint: Even incomplete or marked-up ones from decades ago

checklist.title: What the machine does
checklist.hint: And what it's supposed to do that it currently can't

checklist.title: Products and changeovers
checklist.hint: How many recipes, how often you switch

checklist.title: Acceptable downtime window
checklist.hint: Weekend, holiday shutdown, or fully scheduled

checklist.title: Plant standards
checklist.hint: Preferred PLC brand and network, if you have one
